metadata.title: Ghost-Filled Orders: Detecting and Testing Atomicity Violations in Non-Custodial Prediction Markets

evidence.title: Ghost-Filled Orders: Detecting and Testing Atomicity Violations in Non-Custodial Prediction Markets

evidence.abstract: Blockchain based prediction markets combine offchain order management with onchain settlement. This architecture supports user controlled custody, since users keep funds in wallets or smart contracts while submitting signed orders to an offchain order book. However, it creates an atomicity gap. An order may be valid when accepted or matched offchain, but become invalid before the corresponding onchain settlement transaction is executed. This behavior, often called ghost filled orders by the community, can cause trades that appear filled offchain to fail onchain. This paper studies this atomicity gap through a case study of Polymarket. We show how the delay between offchain order acceptance and onchain settlement allows adversaries to invalidate unfavorable orders after observing market outcomes or price movements. We then quantify the scale and financial impact of this behavior over a nine-month period from August 12, 2025, to May 22, 2026, using 1.8 million reverted transactions involving Polymarket official smart contracts. Our analysis separates attacker profit from market and user loss, and develops conservative measurement rules to avoid overclaiming impact. We further develop a methodology for testing other blockchain based prediction markets and apply it to three additional markets. We find that all three are vulnerable to the same class of attack, and that one design enables direct attacker profit. We have reported the findings to all three projects; one project had acknowledged the issue at the time of the study.

evidence.title: When AI Agents Meet MEV: Cross-Chain Arbitrage in the Agentic Economy

evidence.abstract: We study cross-chain arbitrage when autonomous AI agents, rather than humans or bots, are the searchers. We model agents as both arbitrage extractors and Maximal Extractable Value targets, derive the optimal trade size for a risk-averse agent under mean-variance utility with stochastic bridge delays, and formalize multi-chain path selection as a belief-weighted online learning problem whose belief estimates converge under a Robbins-Monro schedule. Using 23,000 Uniswap V3 swap events across Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Base, we find that Ethereum-Arbitrum price gaps average 0.044% at 10-second resolution and Arbitrum--Base gaps average 0.013%, so $10,000 trades clear in 63% of L2-L2 windows via CCTP while L1-L2 routes require $50,000 or more for comparable viability. Our adaptive path-selection algorithm outperforms standard baselines by 11% on average, and moderate randomization cuts MEV exposure by over 50% with only modest profit loss.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Security Is Not Enough: Privacy Gaps in the Renegade Decentralized Dark Pool

evidence.title: Cryptographic Security Is Not Enough: Privacy Gaps in the Renegade Decentralized Dark Pool

evidence.abstract: Dark pools are designed to provide pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality - concealing order flow before execution and limiting information leakage after. Decentralized dark pools, such as Renegade, aim to replicate these properties without custodial risk, using secure multi-party computation (MPC) and zero-knowledge proofs for private order matching and verifiable settlement. We show that Renegade's cryptographic guarantees do not deliver these dark pool properties in practice. MPC-with-abort ensures correctness but not fairness: a party may learn the match result and abort without penalty, breaking pre-trade privacy. We demonstrate that the protocol's discovery layer further leaks trading intent before MPC even begins, and that sustained probing via selective abort can probabilistically reconstruct counterparty order history, threatening post-trade confidentiality. We also show that the absence of input-consistency checks prior to MPC execution enables a griefing attack using invalid state commitments requiring no real token holdings that continuously locks honest users' wallets and wastes compute, breaking liveness under sustained conditions. We further analyze over 700,000 Renegade transactions on Base and probe the P2P layer, finding that the network is effectively centralized: 88% of traffic routes through a handful of relayers, with only four nodes sustaining the P2P layer. Since relayers hold their users' wallet state in plaintext, this concentration means the system operates as a centralized orderbook in practice - reproducing off-chain the information asymmetry that dark pools are designed to eliminate. Together, our results show that cryptographic privacy does not imply dark pool security: pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality each require additional protocol-level guarantees beyond MPC correctness.

metadata.title: EVAGE: Autonomous MEV Generation and Adaptation via Multi-Agent Harness

evidence.title: EVAGE: Autonomous MEV Generation and Adaptation via Multi-Agent Harness

evidence.abstract: Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) has evolved into a major economic force in blockchain ecosystems, yet its capture is dominated by experienced teams, and both strategy design and implementation rely on manual expert work that scales poorly across heterogeneous protocols and chains. We present EVAGE, the first fully autonomous multi-agent framework for end-to-end MEV strategy generation and adaptation. Equipped with three specialized operation modes, it automatically discovers novel MEV variants, adapts execution logic across disparate protocols, and ports strategies between chains, including Layer-1 and Layer-2 networks. To avoid inference latency on the critical MEV execution path, EVAGE generates and refines MEV bot code offline rather than making real-time decisions directly. Under the coordination of an orchestrator agent, three specialized subagents collectively implement and repair the full MEV bot workflow via closed-loop diagnostics, eliminating human intervention while producing validated and deterministic Proof-of-Concept implementations. We evaluate EVAGE on over 1.5M blocks from each of Ethereum, Base, and BNB Smart Chain (BSC). On Ethereum, EVAGE uncovers five novel MEV strategy variants, yielding a profit increase of 1.02$\times$ to 15.97$\times$. It also successfully adapts 11 MEV strategies from CPMM to both CLMM and Balancer V2 and ports strategies from Ethereum to Base and BSC, all with less than 60 dollars in LLM token costs.

metadata.title: Sovereign Grassroots Currencies: A CBDC Architecture for Credit and Monetary Policy (Full Version)

institutions.name: London School of Economics and Political Science

evidence.title: Sovereign Grassroots Currencies: A CBDC Architecture for Credit and Monetary Policy (Full Version)

evidence.abstract: A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is central-bank money in digital form, held by the public. Leading designs have two limitations: conversion from bank deposits into CBDC can accelerate deposit flight, requiring safeguards, and the CBDC stays outside credit creation and monetary-policy operations. Here we present a CBDC architecture based on grassroots currencies that overcomes these limitations. The architecture has three components: (1) Money: sovereign grassroots coins, which are digital debts of one unit of fiat currency issued by the central bank, constituting a direct CBDC; (2) Credit and Liquidity: non-sovereign grassroots coins, which are digital debts of one unit of the same fiat currency, redeemable at par, that can be issued by any person, natural or legal, thus adding credit; and (3) Interest: grassroots bonds, sovereign and non-sovereign, adding maturity and thus interest, standard banking instruments, and the central bank's instruments of monetary policy. The central bank can therefore lend, absorb liquidity, set its rates and buy and sell securities in the coins and bonds the public holds, choosing the counterparties and terms of its credit operations, and without converting bank deposits into newly issued central bank money on demand. We prove that the arbitrage-free price of any non-sovereign grassroots coin whose issuer redeems it on demand is one unit of the fiat currency. The central bank can choose to deal with any counterparty, not just banks, and we argue that the central bank's interest rates on lending and bonds bound from above and below the corresponding interest rates of its counterparties. Sovereign and non-sovereign grassroots coins and bonds have been implemented and tested on a small scale.

metadata.title: Pricing the DeFi Tail: Do Protocols or Depositors Price Operational Risk?

institutions.name: ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences

evidence.title: Pricing the DeFi Tail: Do Protocols or Depositors Price Operational Risk?

institutions.name: ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences

evidence.abstract: Similar to banks, DeFi protocols expose depositors to operational risk (USD 9.45 billion across 1,075 events since 2020). Unlike banks, they are not required to hold capital against it. A protocol may maintain a buffer voluntarily. Absent one, the risk falls on the depositor, who should then demand a risk premium in the supply yield. I quantify the underlying tail on one benchmark, a per-sector Basel loss-distribution approach fitted to a new operational risk event dataset, and test both margins against it. Tails in the four core sectors are no heavier than the Moscadelli banking band $[0.85, 1.39]$. Bridge, Derivatives, and the residual Other sector exhibit cyber-loss-level tails ($\hatξ\approx 1.6$), with point estimates past the infinite-mean boundary. The Lending tail implies a $\mathrm{VaR}_{99.9}$ capital buffer of 18% of TVL and of the ten largest Lending venues, the four holding a buffer cover on average 5% of it. Under market discipline, depositors should demand a higher yield in compensation where a venue does not maintain a buffer. I find that venues without a buffer pay a higher premium than those with (a 125-bps gap in medians): evidence the market discriminates in the right direction. However, the premium falls far short of an adequately priced tail. This unpriced tail falls disproportionately on the retail depositor, who sees only the posted rate but lacks the information and skills to price it. Because these products are not bank-regulated, I recommend disclosure over capital mandates: protocols, and any service providers that front access to it, should publish standardized losses, existing capital buffers and tail coverage.

metadata.title: Breaking Cycles for Scalable Fair Ordering in Blockchain Systems

evidence.title: Breaking Cycles for Scalable Fair Ordering in Blockchain Systems

evidence.abstract: In blockchain systems, transaction order directly determines financial outcomes: unfair ordering enables front-running and sandwich attacks that have extracted over \$686M from Ethereum users. Current fair-ordering protocols aggregate pairwise receive-order evidence from replicas. Under contention or adversarial manipulation, however, Condorcet cycles force them into global strongly connected component (SCC) condensation, causing delays, coarse batches, and scaling failures. We present FlashOrder, a deterministic fair-ordering engine that localizes cyclic ambiguity before it propagates across the batch. FlashOrder embeds pairwise preferences into one-dimensional canonical positions, clusters nearby transactions with a partition hypergraph, and performs hierarchical inter- and intra-cluster serialization, replacing batch-wide SCC condensation with localized sorting and aggregation. Evaluated against Themis (CCS '23) and Rashnu (VLDB '24) on a libhotstuff-based prototype, FlashOrder achieves up to 10.5$\times$ higher throughput than Themis and 4.8$\times$ higher than Rashnu, with the latency gap widening as network scales. In controlled adversarial simulation, it reduces maximum rank displacement by 88.7\%, and under Condorcet attacks it sustains 12.0$\times$ and 9.7$\times$ higher throughput than Themis and Rashnu on average. These results show that localizing cyclic ambiguity yields stronger fairness at substantially higher throughput.

metadata.title: Verifiable Randomness for Blockchain-Based Lottery Systems

evidence.title: Verifiable Randomness for Blockchain-Based Lottery Systems

evidence.abstract: As lotteries and other high-stakes decentralized applications increasingly depend on unpredictable randomness for their operations, the lack of a secure and transparent on-chain random number generator that is verifiable by all participants remains a critical open problem. Various approaches to blockchain-based random number generation have emerged over the years, each with their own strengths and limitations, and have consistently been superseded as blockchain technology evolved. This paper surveys existing approaches to on-chain randomness and proposes a new platform that builds upon the well-known commit-and-reveal scheme while directly addressing its principal vulnerability, the last revealer attack, in which the final participant can withhold their reveal in order to bias or abort the output upon seeing an unfavorable result. We further compare this solution with prior approaches and evaluate its entropy properties. The proposed architecture combines a web-based front-end with a Solidity smart contract deployed on the Polygon 2.0 blockchain. Implemented and tested on the Amoy testnet, the prototype is low-cost and simple to deploy, providing a practical, accessible proof-of-concept for verifiable on-chain randomness.

metadata.title: Exchange Rate Determination for Cryptocurrency Mergers: A Formal Framework

evidence.title: Exchange Rate Determination for Cryptocurrency Mergers: A Formal Framework

evidence.abstract: Many of the thousands of existing cryptocurrencies suffer from declining adoption, low liquidity and weak security, and merging two of them into a single ecosystem is a natural alternative to abandonment. No rigorous framework exists, however, for determining a fair exchange rate in such a merger. Unlike that of a corporation, the value of a cryptocurrency is driven by network effects, so the exchange rate itself influences the value of the merged asset. We extend the exchange-ratio framework of Mainini, Moretto and Visetti [7] by making the merged value endogenous: the exchange rate determines community migration, migration determines (up to user overlap) the post-merger network state, and an axiomatised valuation function assigns a value to that state. The resulting synergy has no predetermined sign, and the bounds of the bargaining region become self-referential in the exchange rate. We prove that no exchange rate at which the merger destroys value preserves wealth, and that the pre-merger price ratio preserves wealth exactly when the merger does not destroy value at that rate. In that case, under explicit threshold conditions, the price ratio satisfies all five of our fairness conditions -- wealth, adoption, security, governance and liquidity preservation -- and, under strict versions of these conditions, the admissible set contains a nondegenerate interval around it, the wealth-admissible set one of explicit width. The network-value laws proposed in the literature, from the linear law to Metcalfe's and its generalised power-law forms, share a convexity property that yields the Lipschitz control behind these estimates. Liquidity emerges as the only non-wealth condition that can disconnect the admissible set.

metadata.title: On-Chain Archaeology of Bitcoin Oracles: Evidence of Use under Limited Observability

evidence.title: On-Chain Archaeology of Bitcoin Oracles: Evidence of Use under Limited Observability

evidence.abstract: Before Ethereum made the "oracle problem" a household term, Bitcoin already had oracles serving as feeds, key-release services, federated signers, and arbiters that carried real value on the main chain. This study traces their use and the changing evidence of oracle activity from early days through July 2026. We combine a complete census of Counterparty betting (1,149 bets), analysis of the full Bitcoin chain through block 958,628, and searches for documented keys from Reality Keys, Orisi, Bitrated, and Oraclize in an 854-million-row public-key index. We also recover DLC oracle records from an archived explorer and live Nostr relays. Two results emerge. First, early contracts remain on-chain, but many event descriptions have disappeared, and protocol encoding and API limitations complicate access to the surviving record. However, for modern DLCs, public oracle announcements can survive even when the contracts using them cannot be identified on-chain. In the script classes examined, the share of spends that reveal no script peaks at 81.9% in 2024 after excluding spends containing inscription data. Second, public registries can give a misleading picture of oracle use. In Counterparty, 95% of pre-2018 sources declaring an oracle fee were never bet on. In Bitrated, 0.1% of archived keys appear on-chain overall, compared with 10 of 19 keys captured in 2014. Sport dominates Counterparty's matched volume, while a daily price series dominates the archived DLC announcements. These findings show how protocol design and data preservation shape the historical record of Bitcoin oracle use.

metadata.title: Price is Only the Symptom: Understanding and Analyzing Economic-State Manipulation Vulnerabilities in DeFi

evidence.title: Price is Only the Symptom: Understanding and Analyzing Economic-State Manipulation Vulnerabilities in DeFi

evidence.abstract: Economic-state manipulation has emerged as a significant security threat to decentralized finance (DeFi), causing substantial financial losses. Existing studies predominantly characterize these attacks as price manipulation, focusing on observable price distortions while overlooking underlying violations of economic-state integrity. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study of Economic-State Manipulation (ESM) vulnerabilities in DeFi. We first curate a diverse dataset comprising 276 real-world attacks and 91 Code4rena audit findings. Based on these cases, we develop a cause-oriented taxonomy comprising four primary categories and eleven subcategories. Our analysis reveals that ESM vulnerabilities extend beyond conventional price manipulation, frequently involving violations of protocol-internal accounting, AMM state consistency, and execution-time constraints. We further investigate the evaluation datasets of six existing studies and find that, although they cover 6-10 vulnerability subcategories, their distributions remain dominated by limited manipulation mechanisms. Furthermore, we systematically evaluate seven representative detection approaches on our dataset. Our results reveal limited coverage, with the best-performing approach identifying only 50.4% of real-world attacks. Through an analysis of false negatives and false positives, we identify fundamental limitations arising from reliance on predefined attack patterns, insufficient reasoning about economic-state semantics, and incomplete exploitability validation. These findings provide empirical insights for developing more generalizable ESM vulnerability detection techniques.

evidence.title: Blockchain Participation Games with Upfront Contribution Commitment

evidence.abstract: Blockchain participation games combine costly entry, random participation selection, and threshold success into consideration. Their retraction variants charge task-completion costs only to selected contributors. We consider committee tasks whose operators reserve costly computing or communication capacity before assignment, so preparation costs are incurred even when that capacity is not selected. We characterize all pure Nash equilibria under homogeneous selection and analyze how heterogeneous selection shapes who commits. We characterize how the homogeneous minimum-outlay reward scheme supports full contribution, where every user commits, as a Nash equilibrium. Moreover, under heterogeneous selection, requiring zero registration reward can increase the minimum outlay. Finally, when full contribution is a positive-welfare social optimum, the homogeneous zero-registration-reward design attains price of stability one; and under independent Bernoulli selection, every full-contribution Nash equilibrium is also a strong equilibrium.

metadata.title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation

evidence.title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation

evidence.abstract: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

evidence.title: An Incentive-Aligned Trust-Centric Coordination Layer for Heterogeneous Blockchain Interoperability

evidence.abstract: The interoperability between permissioned and public blockchains is hampered by asymmetric privacy, trust, and governance assumptions. We propose a coordination architecture that decouples cross-domain trust management and privacy enforcement from underlying blockchain protocols, requiring no protocol-level modifications. The framework integrates cryptographic unlinkability mechanisms with incentive-compatible relay selection, combining stake-weighted participation and temporally accumulated reputation to align economic commitment with sustained correctness. We formalize the adversarial model and derive security and privacy properties for cross-domain coordination, demonstrating robustness against Sybil infiltration, collusion, and strategic stake concentration. Simulation-based analysis characterizes key design trade-offs between quorum thresholds, reputation memory, and anonymity parameters, indicating that privacy-preserving coordination can be achieved without degrading responsiveness or incentive stability when parameters are properly tuned.

metadata.title: Capital Costs Protect the Network: Mining Gap Dynamics in Proof-of-Work Blockchains Under a Stochastic Mempool

evidence.title: Capital Costs Protect the Network: Mining Gap Dynamics in Proof-of-Work Blockchains Under a Stochastic Mempool

evidence.abstract: Proof-of-Work blockchains increasingly rely on transaction fees to keep miners engaged as block subsidies decline. An immediate outcome of this is that miners may sit idle at the start of a round until enough high-fee transactions accumulate in order to make mining worthwhile. This idle period is known as the mining gap. We model the high-fee transaction backlog as a Lindley-type recursion under a two-tier fee market and use its stationary distribution to characterize the mining gap. Under Bitcoin's difficulty-adjustment mechanism, the expected gap grows strictly with the hashpower active on the network and consumes the entire round as that hashpower grows without bound. A free-entry condition determines a unique long-run equilibrium hashpower. Capital cost caps the equilibrium hashpower and prevents the mining gap from occupying the entire round. We further characterize how the block subsidy, transaction fees, and operating cost shape the equilibrium hashpower and the mining gap.

metadata.title: Pump-and-Dump meets Honeypot Tokens: Detection and Analysis of Telegram Bait-and-Trap Schemes

evidence.title: Pump-and-Dump meets Honeypot Tokens: Detection and Analysis of Telegram Bait-and-Trap Schemes

evidence.abstract: While Pump-and-Dump schemes have been extensively studied on centralized exchanges (CEXs), how they operate in decentralized exchanges (DEXs) remains largely unexplored. We monitor 83 Telegram channels used to coordinate Pump-and-Dump campaigns and collect 3,677 events across the BNB Smart Chain and Ethereum. Our analysis reveals that, although these operations superficially resemble CEX-based Pump-and-Dump schemes, their underlying mechanism is fundamentally different. Rather than manipulating prices, organizers orchestrate deceptive Pump-and-Dump campaigns around honeypot tokens whose smart contracts allow Telegram subscribers to buy but prevent them from selling. Unaware of this restriction, victims purchase these tokens and are unable to recover their funds. We refer to this new fraud mechanism as Bait-and-Trap. We show that Bait-and-Trap provides a substantially more reliable profit strategy than Pump-and-Dump schemes: organizers gain in 99.3% of cases, extracting over $7 million in profit. To counter this threat, we develop a transaction-simulation tool that detects honeypot tokens before purchase by testing whether a user can successfully sell against the token's live contract state, providing a practical defense against Bait-and-Trap operations.

metadata.title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets

evidence.title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets

evidence.abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \$0.04-\$0.21.

metadata.title: Quantifying Observable High-Frequency Swapping on Arbitrum

evidence.title: Quantifying Observable High-Frequency Swapping on Arbitrum

evidence.abstract: Layer-2 rollups have reshaped Ethereum's transaction economy by replacing mempool competition with deterministic sequencing, sub-second block times, and negligible gas fees. While these properties suppress classical Miner/Maximal Extractable Value (MEV), they give rise to a new and previously unrecognized behavioral regime. In this paper, we introduce the concept of High-Frequency Swapping (HFS), referring to continuous single-hop swaps at machine cadence within decentralized exchanges. Despite its growing footprint, this phenomenon has not been systematically identified or quantified in prior work. We conduct a large-scale measurement of HFS on Arbitrum, using 18 months of full-chain data (Jan. 2023--Jun. 2024). Specifically, we construct a reproducible pipeline that isolates voluntary single-swap transactions, attributes them to the swapper level, and classifies HFS behavior through inter-arrival dynamics. The analysis uncovers 477 distinct HFS swappers responsible for nearly 30 million swaps and over $10^{11}$ USD in notional volume. Our study conducts a comprehensive empirical investigation of HFS from multiple perspectives. We begin with a global overview of activity patterns, and then examine temporal dynamics, swapper identity, token coverage, and venue concentration, and explore swap size, time gap, and order direction. Finally, we explore case-level behavior, including stablecoin arbitrage, CEX-DEX execution gaps, and short-horizon round-trip trading. Across these dimensions, we identify consistent structural regularities that distinguish HFS from conventional retail or arbitrage activity. This work provides a large-scale address-level empirical characterization of High-Frequency Swapping on Arbitrum and a broad empirical foundation for future research on decentralized market microstructure.

metadata.title: A game-theoretic analysis of the market microstructure in decentralized exchanges with concentrated liquidity

evidence.title: A game-theoretic analysis of the market microstructure in decentralized exchanges with concentrated liquidity

evidence.abstract: We study strategic liquidity provision in decentralized exchanges with concentrated liquidity as a mean-field game. Liquidity providers choose the width of their price range and when to rebalance it, pay a transaction cost at each rebalancing, and share the fees collected at each tick in proportion to their liquidity, so that each provider's income depends on the state of the population. We formulate the problem as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space. In an averaged version of the game, in which a rebalanced position is re-centered at a draw from the long-run law of the price, a mean-field equilibrium exists. Because each provider's share of the fees falls as competing liquidity is added, the equilibrium liquidity profile is unique. For the exact dynamics, with rebalancing at the range boundary and fast execution, we obtain closed forms for the optimal width, the value function and the stationary law of a position, together with a critical volatility above which provision does not pay. Free entry holds a pool strictly below this threshold, at a margin set by the rebalancing cost. The critical volatility is computed from the fee tier, traded volume, active-tick liquidity and price alone, with no fitted parameter. On two and a half years of hourly data from five WETH/USDC pools on Ethereum and Base, it tracks realized volatility. On the Ethereum $0.3\%$ pool the ratio of realized to critical volatility is less than one, and optimal value $w^*$ exists. On the standard Uniswap fee tiers the critical volatility coincides with the on-chain implied volatility of the pool.

metadata.title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market

evidence.title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market

evidence.abstract: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs'' per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.

metadata.title: NEST: Stale-Robust Tokenized-Stock Measurement for a Crypto-Treasury LETF Stack

evidence.title: NEST: Stale-Robust Tokenized-Stock Measurement for a Crypto-Treasury LETF Stack

evidence.abstract: Tokenized equities trade while listed markets are closed, so their marks could improve off-hours measurement along layered exposures that link Bitcoin, crypto-treasury stocks, and leveraged ETFs. A token return and the next opening gap, however, share the price move from the previous close to the token mark, so part of their apparent fit is mechanical. We develop NEST, a stale-robust protocol that separates this shared-history fit from conditional measurement value. A shared-history identity and a variance-clock bound show how much fit timing alone can generate. The partial determination index (PDI), the squared partial correlation between token and gap given public controls, measures what remains, and a finite-sample frontier expresses the partial-F decision in PDI units. Product, provenance, timestamp, and execution audits decide whether an informative mark is admissible. For MSTRx, a tracker certificate on MicroStrategy (MSTR), a token-only $R^2$ of 0.916 shrinks to a modest increment once Bitcoin, mark age, and a pre-09:00 MSTR premarket proxy are controlled: the token explains 15.7% of the remaining gap variation (1% frontier 0.031), and 14.0% to 17.0% under stricter clock variants, including one in which every token mark precedes 09:00. A trade-level reconstruction on Gate gives 25.2%; NVDAX and AAPLX clear their frontiers, whereas TSLAX does not. An admitted mark updates, rather than replaces, BTC-unit exposure diagnostics for the BTC-MSTR-LETF chain.

metadata.title: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending

evidence.title: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending

evidence.abstract: We propose a lending protocol with far fewer risks than existing pool-based lending protocols (e.g., Aave, Compound). In our protocol, lenders and borrowers embody the spirit of decentralization by making competing interest-rate offers, resulting in the discovery of the prevailing interest rate through tâtonnement-like dynamics as opposed to taking rates partly determined by a central authority (e.g., Aave, Federal Reserve). We eliminate the risk of manipulation by creating loans with a fixed interest rate throughout the loan---like US Treasury bills. In particular, we further derive performance guarantees probabilities of repayment shortfall and liquidation by modeling the value of the collateral as a random walk, thus allowing participants to more efficiently manage their risk. To do so, we use characteristic functions and Fourier inversion to derive exact integral representations of the liquidation and repayment shortfall probabilities under the most general assumptions. We illustrate empirically this method by using Bitcoin as collateral and fitting its historical prices to Gaussian, Student-$t$, and symmetric stable Paretian distributions.

metadata.title: When Token Transfers Do Not Mean Liquidity in Tokenized Real-World Assets

evidence.title: When Token Transfers Do Not Mean Liquidity in Tokenized Real-World Assets

evidence.abstract: On-chain transfer volume is often used to describe activity in tokenized real-world assets (RWAs), although recorded transfers may reflect very different economic functions, including token creation, destruction, issuer-related operations, and movements between other addresses. Ownership measures face a similar problem because a large address balance may belong to a pool or intermediary that represents multiple investors. We address these two measurement problems by decomposing transfer activity and making ownership coverage explicit. Transfer turnover is calculated before and after observable event categories are separated, using the same asset, observation window, and supply denominator. For ownership, we compare concentration measured against total supply with concentration among the addresses that remain after identified intermediaries are excluded. Using Ethereum-based tokenized funds from December 2025 to August 2026, we find that transfer classification can materially change measured turnover. We also show that removing an intermediary can lower concentration when measured against total supply while concentration among the remaining addresses increases. Transfer activity and address concentration need to be interpreted with their underlying transaction functions and ownership coverage in mind. These measures provide evidence about liquidity-related activity, but they do not directly measure market liquidity. The code and data used in the analysis are available at https://github.com/atytmr07/rwa-liquidity.

evidence.abstract: Many decentralized exchanges use automated market makers (AMMs) to trade assets against liquidity pools. Modern AMMs allow third-party contracts, called Hooks, to customize this process. However, Hooks can impose additional deductions that fee breakdowns based on standard pool parameters do not itemize. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale empirical study of the production Hook ecosystem, focusing on these undisclosed settlement charges. Our study covers 7,873 Hook deployments, 50,011 pools, and 296M pool events on Uniswap v4 and PancakeSwap Infinity across Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain (BSC) through August 1, 2026. We develop a bytecode analysis that reconstructs how Hooks change traders' payments and receipts, separating charges from exchanged assets and standard fees. We then reconstruct historical settlements to measure charging frequency and economic burden. We find that direct settlement adjustment is the dominant Hook capability, supported by 71.37% of registered Hooks. Charging capability is widespread and often exercised: 24.30% of Hooks can impose undisclosed deductions, and these deductions occur in 59.23% of accounted swaps involving such Hooks. These charges generate millions of dollars in revenue, with $3.97M recorded across Hooks with available token prices. These findings reveal a gap between standard fee displays and actual trading costs, motivating explicit disclosure of Hook deductions alongside standard fees.

metadata.title: Manipulation-Resistant Oracles via Continuous Peer Prediction

evidence.title: Manipulation-Resistant Oracles via Continuous Peer Prediction

evidence.abstract: Blockchain oracle networks, including decentralised physical infrastructure networks (DePINs), report physical measurements from a source that can manipulate the underlying process. A carbon project operator, for example, can dry a site before measurement and be paid for soil organic carbon (SOC) that was never stored. Peer prediction covers discrete signals under a strategic source, or continuous reports under an honest source, but not both at once. We close that gap for Gaussian reports. Strict propriety of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) settles the reporting stage alone. Our result concerns the source stage. A report-only settlement rule whose honest-source payoff is non-decreasing in the true value identifies and deters source manipulation if and only if the sensors respond to that manipulation by different amounts. When they respond identically, manipulation is observationally equivalent to a genuine rise in SOC, and CRPS translation equivariance leaves every peer score unchanged, so no such rule deters the source. Necessity follows from invariance rather than from the signal enumeration available in the discrete case. The source-stage estimator is ordinary weighted least squares, and the contribution is the characterisation around it. With eight calibrated SOC models on 37,280 real European soil spectra, shift-naive aggregators over-credit by up to 57% under a calibrated moisture perturbation while the joint estimate stays near-unbiased. The guarantee holds on the equilibrium path for non-colluding reporters and inherits the models' own calibration error. The project page is at https://rqcker.github.io/crps-wls.

metadata.title: Resolution is not Settlement, Part I: Oracle Adjudication and Semantic Governance on Polymarket

evidence.title: Resolution is not Settlement, Part I: Oracle Adjudication and Semantic Governance on Polymarket

evidence.abstract: Prediction-market resolution is often reduced to a terminal outcome and one timestamp. That representation is inadequate for leveraged event claims because rule versioning, request creation, proposal, dispute, reset, Oracle finality, and adapter terminality are distinct states with different observation precision and balance-sheet consequences. We reconstruct those states for Polymarket using Oracle request generations as the unit of adjudication. The population is frozen at Polygon block 79,721,080 and contains 185,550 initialized adapter-question instances and 350,703 decoded adapter logs. Exact requester-filtered extraction yields 504,332 decoded Oracle lifecycle events: 184,148 request creations, 159,447 proposals, 1,604 disputes, and 159,133 settlements. The accounting closes as 182,671 questions with at least one request plus 1,477 successor generations. Immutable chain identity and deployed request semantics provide exact linkage; unfinished histories remain right-censored. Request age is not semantic resolution age. Median request-to-first-proposal time is 182 seconds on the legacy route but 176,388-744,151 seconds on modern routes; post-reset successor proposals arrive within 300-2,909 seconds at the median. This descriptive contrast does not establish causal efficiency. Exact stable-ID metadata linkage recovers 104,032 of 185,550 questions (56.07%), leaves 81,518 unmatched, and produces no ambiguous exact match. External-source publication and contractual-decidability clocks remain unmeasured population-wide and are not replaced by mechanism timestamps. The results establish an event-sourced account of Oracle adjudication, semantic governance, and adapter terminality. Companion Part II reconstructs Conditional Tokens payout recording and observed redemption, preserving the boundary between adjudication, protocol settlement, and holder realization.

metadata.title: Resolution is not Settlement, Part II: Protocol Finality and Observed Redemption on Polymarket

evidence.title: Resolution is not Settlement, Part II: Protocol Finality and Observed Redemption on Polymarket

evidence.abstract: An Oracle result is not yet a protocol payout, a redeemable position is not yet collateral in a holder's account, and a redemption event is not a complete measure of economic entitlement. This companion paper develops an event-sourced framework for Polymarket conditions from preparation through protocol finality and observed holder realization. The empirical design uses three Conditional Tokens Framework event families derived from a pinned contract application binary interface (ABI): ConditionPreparation, ConditionResolution, and PayoutRedemption. It separates the contract-wide acquisition universe from the frozen Polymarket adapter-question cohort. The exact bridge contains 108,638 linked conditions. Of these, 99,283 have an observed protocol-resolution event by the fixed snapshot at Polygon block 90,114,204 (2026-07-12T17:11:41Z). Among resolved exact-linked conditions, 92,158 have an observed redemption of any amount and 91,817 have an observed positive-payout redemption; condition-specific Kaplan-Meier medians from first protocol resolution are 182 and 200 seconds respectively. The exact-linked payout taxonomy contains 53,847 canonical (0,1) vectors, 45,024 canonical (1,0) vectors, 410 fifty-fifty vectors, two other valid vectors, and 9,355 conditions with no observed resolution. Cross-contract Oracle-adapter-protocol ordering is reported conservatively: 823 conditions have an interval-qualified terminal generation, 48 have multiple candidate generations, 91,638 have no compatible terminal generation in the frozen evidence, and 16,129 are right-censored or otherwise unevaluable. The formal results show that Oracle finality does not identify protocol finality, protocol finality does not identify holder realization, and redemption events alone do not identify the fraction of entitlement redeemed without an independent balance-consistent entitlement denominator.

metadata.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana

evidence.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana

evidence.abstract: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.

metadata.title: Who Aggregates Information? Screening, Rent, and the Coexistence of CLOB and AMM Prediction Markets

evidence.title: Who Aggregates Information? Screening, Rent, and the Coexistence of CLOB and AMM Prediction Markets

evidence.abstract: Prediction-market shares differ from traditional financial products in that, with no information or outside utility, classical delta-neutral Central Limit Order Book~(CLOB) market making cannot be financed by payoff-uninformative noise flow. Transaction-level evidence from a major prediction-market CLOB platform shows makers profiting not from spread but from carrying an under-priced side to settlement --- the empirical signature of behavioral tail demand rather than classical, randomized noise. We build this tail demand directly into the model and study an LMSR and a CLOB on the same event. A pre-shock CLOB quote inside the common-signal band is picked off; competitive quotes therefore screen informed traders out of the book. CLOB makers earn screening rent by carrying the under-priced side to resolution, while informed flow routes to the LMSR. The venues coexist: the CLOB supplies the tail-demand rent margin that lets the LMSR recover part of its loss to informed flow, and AMM depth moves the CLOB premium with a sign set by maker-side contestability---widening it where standing quotes can be undercut, compressing it where a committed maker carries the book. With three or more outcomes, binary-book CLOBs pin switch prices but leave implied beliefs indeterminate, whereas the LMSR prices the outcome simplex coherently and uses collateral more efficiently.

metadata.title: Herding or Racing? Decomposing Cross-Account Order-Flow Persistence in On-Chain Markets

evidence.title: Herding or Racing? Decomposing Cross-Account Order-Flow Persistence in On-Chain Markets

evidence.abstract: Most of the autocorrelation in trade signs on decentralized exchanges comes from pairs of trades sent by different wallets. For Uniswap v3, this has been read as herding dominating order splitting -- the reverse of what equity markets show. We show that this herding share mixes two quantities: the probability $p$ that consecutive orders come from the same account, which is small when thousands of wallets are trading, and the ratio $κ$ of cross-account to same-account sign correlation. For any $p$, $κ$ equals one under the public-signal benchmark of Tóth et al. and zero under independent order splitting. On Uniswap v3 USDC-WETH (one week each in 2023 and 2024), the herding share is 0.65-0.86, but $κ$ is only 0.05-0.10. On a fully on-chain EVM limit order book, the herding share is similar (0.61-0.87), but $κ$ is 0.72-0.76; among Uniswap swaps above USD 100k, it is 0.34-0.52. Where $κ$ is high, cross-account co-movement is mostly a race for the price on a centralized exchange. It is concentrated in orders a few blocks apart, and a cross-fitted gradient-boosted filter that sees only Binance data removes about three quarters or more of it. This race flow accounts for most of the losses of liquidity providers. We recommend reporting $κ$ alongside the herding share and modeling on-chain order flow as splitting traders plus arbitrageurs who respond to the centralized-exchange price.

metadata.title: Dynamics of the Liquidity Profile in Concentrated Liquidity Provision: An SPIDE Approach

evidence.title: Dynamics of the Liquidity Profile in Concentrated Liquidity Provision: An SPIDE Approach

evidence.abstract: We model the dynamics of the liquidity profile in Uniswap~V3 and other concentrated-liquidity automated market makers with a stochastic partial integro-differential equation (SPIDE). The profile, the aggregate of all provider positions across tick space, evolves under a degenerate Sturm--Liouville operator, which encodes mean-reverting concentration around the market price, coupled with a Hilbert--Schmidt integral operator, which captures nonlocal redistribution driven by provider repositioning. We establish existence and uniqueness of the mild solution in a weighted $L^2$ space built on the Gegenbauer eigensystem, and reduce the SPIDE to a coupled system of linear stochastic differential equations whose low-order modes describe the level, slope, and curvature of the profile. Pairing the SPIDE with a log-price process yields tractable expressions for pool reserves, pool value, and loss-versus-rebalancing under Ornstein--Uhlenbeck-type and Black--Scholes-type noise. A finite-rank calibration in a fixed reference frame, applied to three Uniswap pools, gives interpretable estimates and lowers active-band forecast error relative to a martingale benchmark on the two pools compatible with the stationary specification. On the third pool, out-of-sample diagnostics are consistent with nonstationarity, which motivates price-aware and time-varying extensions.

metadata.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets

evidence.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets

evidence.abstract: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

metadata.title: Loss-versus-rebalancing with external proportional transaction costs

evidence.title: Loss-versus-rebalancing with external proportional transaction costs

evidence.abstract: We study liquidity provision in automated market makers when trading in the external market incurs proportional transaction costs. We consider both separately collected fees and fees retained in reserves. The benchmark is a self-financing strategy holding the same total risky inventory and trading at the external bid and ask. Under continuous external prices and pure arbitrage, the pool and benchmark have identical liquidation wealth whenever the pool fee or the external spread is positive. Thus loss-versus-rebalancing relative to this transaction-cost benchmark is zero, even without a pool fee if the external spread is positive. We then construct retained-fee utility-indifference pools that implement admissible decreasing inventory schedules, and geometric mean pools that implement feasible constant no-trade boundaries for portfolio weights. These results offer an investment interpretation of liquidity provision: by choosing the pool design, a liquidity provider can specify a trading strategy whose rebalancing is carried out by arbitrageurs.

metadata.title: Oracle-Parametrized Constant Function Market Makers: From Price Feeds to Pricing Rules

evidence.title: Oracle-Parametrized Constant Function Market Makers: From Price Feeds to Pricing Rules

evidence.abstract: This paper introduces oracle-parametrized automated market makers (OP-AMMs), i.e., automated market makers whose quoted price depends jointly on the pool reserves and an external oracle price. In doing so, we extend the information-agnostic AMM framework to settings, such as tokenized securities, for which price discovery occurs off-chain. Under a strict oracle-contraction condition, we show that the quoted price of any OP-AMM interpolates between the oracle price and an implicit autarkic price determined by the pool reserves. We then derive a general loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR) decomposition that separates the residual exposure to market lags from the losses induced by oracle errors. This analysis is further extended to stale, discrete-update oracles and to sandwich attacks around oracle updates. Using this framework, we find conditions under which OP-AMMs simultaneously increase local capital efficiency and reduce normalized LVR relative to information-agnostic AMMs. However, sufficiently noisy or stale oracles can reverse these gains. A counterfactual backtest using one-second SPY NBBO data is provided to demonstrate these trade-offs. In particular, we map the Pareto-efficient frontier of oracle-parametrized constant function market maker (OP-CFMM) designs across stylized oracle regimes.

metadata.title: Non-Convex Market Makers: Coherence without Convexity, Friction, and Parallel Composition

evidence.title: Non-Convex Market Makers: Coherence without Convexity, Friction, and Parallel Composition

evidence.abstract: Cost-function market makers are always assumed convex, and convexity is not what makes them coherent. For a path-independent maker the exact no-arbitrage condition is a chord condition, that every chord slope of the cost lie in the convex hull of payoffs; convexity enters the standard axiomatics through a separate requirement, monotone information incorporation, and dropping it leaves coherent non-convex makers. Rational flow against such a maker trades the convex envelope, so non-convexity costs expressiveness rather than soundness, and a proportional fee of at least the arbitrage depth restores no-arbitrage, which by conjugation is a bid-ask spread with an exact no-trade interval for any cost whatever. Combining fee-bearing makers is an infimal convolution solved by one monotone clearing-price root-find, with sparse participation and a consolidated limit order book as the aggregate, and a deep quadratic co-quoter is Moreau smoothing, which preserves coherence at every depth. Any quoted configuration outside the coherent hull admits a portfolio priced below its worst payoff, so arbitrageurs act as decentralized separation oracles, and coherence is relative to friction and to the cost of finding certificates.

metadata.title: The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket

evidence.abstract: The favorite--longshot bias (FLB) is one of the most persistent return patterns in betting markets, but its prevalence in modern prediction markets and its relation to recurrent longshot demand remain unclear. We study these questions in Polymarket, a large and increasingly important prediction market, using 588 million trades by 2.48 million accounts. In observed transaction flows, purchases below 10 cents lose 19.3 cents per dollar, while purchases at or above 90 cents earn 0.83 cents. How contracts are grouped changes the result: longshots lose 6.3 cents per dollar when each contract is weighted equally but gain 4.1 cents when related contracts are first grouped by parent event; the two-sided pattern is robust in Crypto and Politics but surprisingly absent in Sports. The top decile of accounts with the strongest past tendency to buy longshots accounts for 26.6 percent of next-month low-price purchases, but earns similar returns to others. The top decile of accounts with the strongest past tendency to buy favorites accounts for 15.1 percent of next-month high-price purchases but earns less than others. These findings provide evidence of an aggregate FLB on Polymarket, but its magnitude depends on how contracts are grouped.

metadata.title: A PRELUDE TO THE THEORY OF REAL-WORLD ASSET (RWA) TOKENIZATION

evidence.abstract: We provide an introduction to real-world asset (RWA) tokenization, and develop two economic models connecting this emerging market to classical financial theory. In search for a theory of RWA tokenization, we classify RWA tokenization according to the role of the underlying asset, distinguishing standard RWA tokenization, stablecoins, and Digital Asset Treasuries (DATs). Our first model connects tokenization with security design under asymmetric information. Continuous secondary-market trading generates information recovery, reducing adverse-selection costs over time and affecting both the issuance price and the optimal tokenization design. Our second model develops a dynamic corporate-finance framework for DATs, in which market valuation, capital-market financing, and crypto accumulation interact endogenously. We characterize the optimal issuance policy and illustrate the model using \texttt{Strategy} as a case study. A few directions for future research are discussed, providing a starting point for further theoretical and empirical study of RWA markets.

metadata.title: Measuring Trade Direction in a Prediction Market: Settlement Ground Truth and Trading-Cost Measurement on Polymarket

evidence.abstract: Trade-sign errors can change measured trading costs even when classification accuracy is high. We validate the side of Polymarket's public trade prints against the taker leg of each print's on-chain settlement. On twelve selected days between April and August 2026, spanning both exchange generations, 92.1% to 100.0% of prints match a settled taker leg, with exact side and token agreement on all 24.5 million matched pairs. Mint-and-merge settlement makes that taker leg essential: pooling maker and taker legs changes the measured buy share. Signing the full cached tape before settlement selection yields 16.6 million prints signed by every rule; equal-day balanced accuracy is 0.942 for Lee-Ready, 0.768 for the tick test and 0.670 for retrospective bulk volume classification. On 16.4 million identical eligible fills, Lee-Ready raises effective spread by 0.429 cents per share under equal-fill weights; its realised-spread difference is -0.209 cents. Under share-volume weights, taker five-minute midpoint impact is 0.689 cents, while tick and bulk classifications give -0.374 and -0.119 cents. That aggregate sign reversal disappears when tied print rows are excluded. Distortion depends on error-weighted signed outcomes, sample selection and weighting. Receipt-time ordering and unobserved future-quote age limit these delivered-quote accounting quantities; they do not identify causal impact or private information. Supporting venue and collector analyses provide descriptive diagnostics.

metadata.title: Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration as a Composable Solana Primitive

evidence.abstract: Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.

metadata.title: Pricing the Unprovable: Ambiguity, Turnstile Runs, and the Verifiability Discount in Crypto Protocols

evidence.locator: Official archive record; unrefereed preprint

metadata.title: Pricing the Unprovable: Ambiguity, Turnstile Runs, and the Verifiability Discount in Crypto Protocols

evidence.abstract: Privacy-preserving protocols can repair a vulnerability without establishing whether it was exploited beforehand, even when no theft is reported and aggregate supply is protected. We call the potential value reduction from this gap the verifiability discount. A turnstile model shows how early withdrawal can shift a possible shortfall to remaining holders and why credible evidence can become more valuable as exposure grows. We introduce VDISC, a reproducible framework that records reported loss, exposed value, public evidence, returns, and pool flows separately. It combines Orchard's staged disclosures with reconstructed on-chain flows, earlier Zcash cases, and a 40-event security panel. Orchard follows the predicted direction: market responses were muted after repair and supply assurance, while the largest negative return and aggregate shielded-pool net outflow aligned with the acknowledgment that past abuse could not be ruled out. These patterns are directional, not causal. Across events, market-cap-normalized reported loss and unresolved exposure overlap among the 38 events with a public loss figure (Pearson 0.86, Spearman 0.56), partly because exposure is often coded from the loss itself, so returns alone cannot distinguish reported loss from unresolved history. The findings motivate three candidate design priorities: produce privacy-compatible evidence about past states, limit the state exposed by a single flaw, and disclose residual uncertainty explicitly.

metadata.title: Basis-Only Funding Is Not Dividend Fair: Settlement Design in Crypto Equity Perpetuals

evidence.abstract: Crypto venues increasingly list perpetual futures on equities and other real-world assets (RWAs), which trade continuously yet reference dividend-paying stocks: a long equity perpetual marked to the ex-dividend cash price bears the ex-dividend drop without receiving the dividend. We ask whether the premium-index funding architecture these venues run -- funding set from the contemporaneous basis $e_t=P_t-S_t$ rather than a carry target -- can replicate shareholder cash flows for traders entering and exiting at arbitrary times. It cannot. Funding serves two roles that coincide for non-dividend crypto assets but split apart for equities: basis control and settlement. We give the fair-funding identity, cast timing fairness as an optimal-stopping condition, and characterize when the basis is a sufficient statistic for the fair target. The decisive obstruction is measure-theoretic: a predictable dividend is an atom, and no absolutely continuous funding path can replicate an atom over holding intervals even in the weak limit, so fairness must match the atom with an atom -- an event credit. Exchange-native data confirm this: at each covered ex-date one venue posts a discrete funding atom equal to $-D/(\mathrm{Mark}-D)$ while a standard premium-index venue posts none, transferring the dividend across venues -- from native funding alone, with no external spot.

metadata.title: Identity Amortization: Shared Resources and the Cost of Sybil Attacks

evidence.abstract: Sybil defenses commonly price identities by requiring a resource for each one. When one resource can support several identities, an adversary can pay less per identity than the defense intends. We call this identity amortization: a strict reduction in the minimum cost of provisioning identities when resources may be shared, relative to provisioning each one independently. It is a second route to the gap that a Sybil attack exploits. When influence is assigned per identity, a defense calibrated to the nominal price can overestimate the cost of a Sybil threshold by up to the number of identities one resource supports. For any resource catalogue, we give exact tests for when identity amortization occurs, where it begins, and its largest error; a sharing cap below the onset removes it. Because the tests need only prices and capacities, they apply to any defense that admits identities against a shareable resource, telling designers whether the assumed per-identity cost is paid, how wrong it can be, and which intervention restores it most cheaply for honest participants. On published phone-verification prices, per-account estimates overstate provisioning cost 1.6 to 4.3 times; Tor's raised per-address relay limit cut modeled attack cost by 8 to 72%, depending on the address-to-relay price ratio.

evidence.locator: Official archive record; unrefereed preprint

metadata.title: Trim: Fee Level Matters More Than Skew in Lightning Routing

evidence.abstract: Lightning routing nodes lend their channel balance for a posted fee. Operators' tools move that fee with the balance around a hand-set level, and which part of the fee drives revenue is unclear. We present Trim, which models a channel as a two-sided inventory with costly refills. Its optimal fee is a level, set by demand and replenishment, plus a balance skew, the shadow price of liquidity. The level is first order: no fee rule beats the ceiling demand and replenishment set, and on exactly solved channels the best flat fee comes within $1.6\%$ of the optimum at the median, whereas a level off by a factor of two loses tens of percent. The skew is second-order insurance: it adds at most what the flow-balancing flat fee loses to refused forwards. So the level should be chosen: Trim's rule traces the revenue--success frontier, posts one level on every channel, and adds a skew only where refills stay frequent and costly. On a 2026 snapshot with synthetic payments, no tuned tool beats that frontier by over a few percent, and a skew changes gross revenue by a few percent.

metadata.title: Power Adjusting Games Under Block-Dependent Pool Payout Schemes

evidence.abstract: Advanced power adjusting block withholding attacks such as PAW and T-PAW have been analyzed so far under a global-reset version of the proportional scheme (GRP), which is rarely used in practice. In this paper, we analyze T-PAW, which contains FAW and PAW as special cases, under the block-dependent payout schemes deployed in practice: Pay-Per-Last-N-Shares (PPLNS), round-based Proportional (PROP) and exponential-decay (EXP). We derive the revenue ratios analytically, by renewal arguments for PPLNS and through the stationary carry process of an open round for PROP and EXP. We further introduce Power Adjusting Hopping (PAH), where an adversary of any size adjusts its power allocation towards the pool according to the blockwork age of the round without withholding any block, and derive its revenue ratios under PROP and EXP. We show that GRP misestimates the T-PAW gain in a scheme-dependent direction: it overstates the gain under PROP up to an order of magnitude and understates it under EXP for the original slush decay rate. PROP is highly vulnerable to PAH, while EXP faces a trade-off: a slow decay invites PAH and a fast decay invites T-PAW. PPLNS is the least vulnerable scheme: it is immune to PAH and it mitigates, but does not eliminate, T-PAW. All analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations.

metadata.title: Quantifying Repair Risk in Crypto Option Surfaces

evidence.abstract: Option desks adjust crypto option quotes into price surfaces that remain within bid-ask intervals and satisfy standard no-arbitrage restrictions across strikes before computing Greeks, hedge quantities, or risk measures. For the same quote panel, however, these constraints may admit multiple such surfaces, which we call admissible repairs, with different downstream outputs. We define the resulting variation as repair risk and propose repair-risk validation, a matched framework for quantifying dispersion in Greeks, hedge quantities, and risk measures. The mechanism is finite-difference amplification: two admissible repairs within price distance $\varepsilon$ can differ in local normalized-strike curvature by $4\varepsilon/h^2$, where $h$ is local normalized-strike spacing. We evaluate repair risk on Deribit BTC and ETH option chains, using $L_1$ and $L_2$ projections of midpoint prices onto the same admissible set as matched controls. Across 108 matched evaluations spanning 18 sampled calendar months, the median 90th percentile of the scaled spot-gamma gap for $L_2$ versus the $ρ=10$ smoothness-penalized repair is nearly twenty times the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control. We also instantiate NN-Proj, a neural-projection repair, to test whether learned repairs exhibit repair risk. Despite good held-out fit, its downstream outputs remain distinct from those of classical repairs. Across five seeds with the same training window and architecture, its curvature dispersion exceeds the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control in 17 of 18 months ($p=1.45\times10^{-4}$). For a USD 1 million risk reversal, switching from $L_2$ to the $ρ=10$ repair shifts the median 90th-percentile hedge notional by 18.62 basis points of gross spot notional. VaR-style estimates also exhibit greater dispersion across repairs. The repair rule is therefore part of the risk model, not merely a feasibility check.

metadata.title: Beyond Identity Creation: Bilinear Sybil Cost in Identities and Time

evidence.abstract: Sybil defenses price the creation of an identity, yet influence goes, again and again, to active identities. We study the cost of maintaining influence. A defense has a bilinear Sybil cost with ratio $A$ if keeping $s$ identities active for $T$ periods costs at least $sT/A$ honest units: the average cost per identity-window is at least $1/A$ times an honest participant's cost. Recurrence alone does not guarantee this cost. The cost can be carried over from earlier periods, shared among many identities, or be negligible when fast hardware does the work of thousands of honest devices. We give four sufficient conditions for a defense that checks every identity each period to achieve bilinear Sybil cost: identity binding, freshness, a shared deadline, and sequential, non-batchable work. They yield two guarantees: a bilinear total cost, with $A$ the speed advantage of the adversary's fastest hardware, and, because the work must be fresh and finished by a common deadline, a bound on the identities active in a period by the processors running at that time. We prove that none of the four follows from the other three. A verifiable delay function on an identity-bound input meets all four without payments, with $A$ of 2 to 8 for CPUs and about 28 for a hypothetical ASIC, against $10^3$ to $10^7$ for hash puzzles. We measure one active identity per core per period against about 80,000 under a signed heartbeat, no gain from batching up to 1,000 identities, and rejection of all tested attacks.

metadata.title: Trustless Bitcoin Vaults

evidence.abstract: Bitcoin (BTC) is the largest crypto asset, yet the Bitcoin blockchain offers few applications in which BTC can be used. A standard approach to make BTC useful is bridging: BTC is deposited on the Bitcoin chain and a wrapped asset is minted on a chain such as Ethereum, where it can be used in smart contract applications. Unfortunately, all Bitcoin bridges to date require trust assumptions on a centralized party or a committee running the bridge to enable withdrawals of the deposited BTC, including state-of-the-art BitVM bridges. In this paper, we observe that while bridges are application-agnostic, most BTC holders are interested in collateral-based applications, where BTC is deposited as collateral, and only the depositor or a set of known counterparties can withdraw the asset. For this class of applications, we propose a primitive, Trustless Bitcoin Vaults, that guarantees that the BTC depositor or the counterparties can withdraw the deposited BTC following only the logic of the application smart contract without trusting any third party. We present a protocol that achieves the security guarantees of this primitive and instantiate it for a lending application where the deposited BTC is used as collateral to borrow against a set of liquidators on the Aave v4 smart contracts on Ethereum. Our mainnet experiments show that at the current Bitcoin price and fee rate, a deposit costs about \$0.7 in fees while a withdrawal costs at most \$7.7. Our construction is built on recent advances in efficient proof verification for Bitcoin.

metadata.title: The Illusion of Payload Blindness: Why MEV Mitigations Fail in Practice

evidence.locator: Official archive record; unrefereed preprint

metadata.title: The Illusion of Payload Blindness: Why MEV Mitigations Fail in Practice

evidence.abstract: In public blockchains, the ability to order visible transactions allows block producers to extract value from users, a problem known as Maximal Extractable Value (MEV). Proposer-Builder Separation has turned that right into a formalized auction, and the leading protocol-level mitigations answer it with payload blindness: encrypted mempools, verifiable permutations, and block delay hide or scramble transactions before the order is fixed. Every such mitigation carries a security argument that assumes an adversary who learns nothing before the order commits. Deployed systems face a different adversary, and this paper measures the cost of that difference. We evaluate the three families of mitigations against a single adversary hierarchy, using closed-form analysis and simulations calibrated to Ethereum. Against a fully blind adversary, the outcome follows from the definitions: encryption with a permutation removes the attack classes that depend on transaction content, and block delay increases extraction rather than reducing it. Once that idealization is dropped, deployment problems dominate. The unencrypted envelope identifies the sender, so past behavior restores a usable guess at hidden content. Optional encryption gives builders a reason to starve the transactions it protects, and voluntary adoption then collapses. Key rotation turns a cryptographic parameter into a source of queueing congestion. Suppressing extraction, finally, removes far more producer revenue than it returns to users in lower fees, so the cost of every mitigation falls on the party that controls its deployment. The binding obstacles to MEV-free blockchains are therefore liveness and deployment incentives rather than cryptography.

metadata.title: Defeating Time-Average Selfish Mining Across Epoch Boundaries in Nakamoto Consensus

evidence.abstract: Selfish mining profits in Nakamoto consensus because difficulty adjustment mechanisms (DAMs) misinterpret uncounted orphans as hash-rate contraction. Although orphan-aware DAMs record orphaned proof-of-work, strict same-epoch inclusion rules enable an orphan exclusion attack (OEA): an adversary can race private forks near epoch boundaries to permanently exclude honest tail orphans from retargeting, restoring substantial profits in short-epoch protocols. We propose the pipelined buffer difficulty adjustment mechanism (PB-DAM), which partitions each epoch into an accountable prefix and a settlement buffer of depth $d$. Pipelining estimation windows across epochs grants honest miners a grace period to report prefix uncles while advancing buffer work to subsequent retargets, closing the boundary gap without heuristic damping. Random-walk excursion bounds demonstrate that OEA success decays exponentially with $d$ for all $\alpha \le \alpha^\star < 1/2$, reducing the time-averaged profit advantage to $O(\varepsilon)$. Under stylized dynamic scheduling models, intermittent idling is analytically shown to be unable to raise the gross reward rate above $\alpha$. Simulations confirm that buffer depths $d = 16$ neutralize selfish mining even at $L = 64$ when $\alpha = 0.40$, and systems recover from a $50\%$ hash-rate crash within $2.2 \pm 0.8$ epochs, incurring under $1\%$ block capacity overhead.
